sections.body:
Dark psychology is the use of a persuasion technique to hide the real terms of a deal. The technique itself is ordinary: people open with an anchor, they mention a deadline, they are pleasant to work with. What makes it dark is the layer built on top of the technique. The real price is not the price you were told. The stock is not as short as you were told. The deadline is not as fixed as you were told. The persuasion is real, and the fact underneath it is not.

So the line between the two is short. A technique changes how a request is presented. Dark psychology changes what the request is really about. Telling a buyer that only two units are left is a technique, and it is a fair one when two units are left. Telling them the same thing when there are forty in the warehouse is the deception, and the sentence does not change.

Pressure is not dark psychology. Both sides of a negotiation carry real limits: a quarter ends, a budget is approved, a line has to start. A seller who says the price goes up on Friday may be telling the truth, and a buyer who says the order has to go out this week may be telling the truth too. The question is never whether the person is honest in general. The question is whether this number, this stock and this date are the ones you would find if you checked them.

This article is written for the side of the desk that has less practice with these sentences. It gives three things: the name of the technique being used, the honest version of the same request, and the two numbers to have ready before you walk in — the alternative, and the price above which you walk away.
examples: The technique was ordinary; the stock count under it was not.
A deadline can be real and still be the wrong thing to accept today.
Name the technique, then ask for the honest version of the same request.
sections.heading: What dark psychology means here

sections.body:
Most of the pressure in a negotiation arrives in one short sentence, and the sentence is repeatable. You do not need to study a method. You need to learn a few sentences and recognise them while they are being said.

Anchoring is the first number, and every number after it is measured against that one. A seller opens high, a buyer opens low, and the opening figure becomes the reference point of the whole conversation. *"The comparable machine last year was 120,000, and this one is a better one."* The honest version of that sentence is a real comparable, with its date and its scope, so that the other side can check it. **Scarcity** is the claim that the supply is short: *"there are two left in stock"*. It is the easiest of the techniques to check, because a number can be counted. Ask how many are left, and ask who counted them.

Urgency shortens the time you have to think: *"the price changes on Friday"*, *"I need an answer before the order closes"*. **Social proof** puts the decision in the hands of a crowd: *"four teams in your company already run this"* — and the crowd is only a crowd if it is a crowd you can check. **Reciprocity** counts a favour. The discount, the free sample, the long demonstration, the spare part that arrives before the invoice: none of these is a gift, and each one is a line in a ledger that the other side expects to be paid back in the price.

None of these five needs a bad person. A decent colleague uses all of them and invents nothing. What the reader has to notice is the gap between the technique and the fact under it: the number that was never the real price, the stock that was never short, the deadline that was never fixed. The gap is where a negotiation turns dark, and the gap is the only thing this article asks you to look for.
examples: The first number is the anchor, and everything after it is measured against that.
How many are left, and who counted them?
Where does the Friday date come from?
A favour is not a gift. It is on the other side of the ledger.
sections.heading: The sentences you will actually hear at a desk

terms.example: The seller opened at 120,000, and every figure after that was measured against it.
terms.gloss: The first number of a negotiation, which every later number is measured against.

terms.example: The scarcity was easy to check: the warehouse held forty, not two.
terms.gloss: The claim that the supply is short, which makes waiting look like a loss.

terms.example: The urgency was plain: answer before Friday and the price holds.
terms.gloss: The shortening of the time you have to think before you decide.

terms.example: It used social proof: four other teams had already bought the same machine.
terms.gloss: The use of other people's decisions as evidence for your own.

terms.example: The discount was the favour, and the renewal at the same price was the bill.
terms.gloss: The pressure to return a favour that the other side has given you.

sections.body:
Four more words are used in the same room, and they matter most when the negotiation moves from the price to the decision itself.

Liking is the pull of a person you like. The supplier who sends the spare part before the invoice, the manager who remembers your name, the engineer who spends twenty minutes on your problem instead of five: liking is a real relationship, and it is not a substitute for terms. **Commitment and consistency** is the pull of your own earlier yes. The small agreement you already made, the specification you signed, the budget you approved: once a person has agreed to one thing, the next agreement is expected to follow from it, and the pressure is on them to behave as if it does.

Loss aversion is the weight a loss carries next to a gain of the same size. This is why *"you are losing 20,000 a month without this"* lands harder than *"you could gain 20,000 with this"*, even when the two numbers are identical. **Framing** is the choice of words around the same fact: a cost of 400 a month or 4,800 a year, a saving or a cost avoided, a risk or a loss. The deal does not change. The frame changes how the deal feels, and a frame can hide what is inside it.

A reader who knows these four words can say what is happening in the room without accusing anybody. Naming the technique moves the conversation back to the facts: the price, the terms, the date.
examples: Liking is a relationship; it is not a substitute for a price.
We already agreed the scope, so let us agree the price on the same basis.
The same number, called a saving in one sentence and a cost in the next.
Name it, then go back to the facts: the price, the terms, the date.
sections.heading: The other words of the trade

terms.example: The liking did not change the price, but it changed who got the last word.
terms.gloss: The pull of a person you like, used to move the decision away from the terms.

terms.example: He had approved the budget, so the second approval came easier.
terms.gloss: The pressure to act in line with what you have already agreed or done.

terms.example: The same 20,000 hurt as a loss and helped as a saving.
terms.gloss: The weight a loss carries compared with a gain of the same size.

terms.example: The framing changed nothing: 400 a month is the same money as 4,800 a year.
terms.gloss: The choice of words around a fact, which changes how the fact feels.

sections.body:
This is the page to keep. The second column is the sentence you will hear; the third is what that sentence does to the price or to the decision; the fourth is the same request made without the pressure.

Read the last column while you prepare, not while you defend. A buyer who has the honest version ready can answer the request and still hold the price, because the answer is about the request and not about the other side.

The two requests in the middle of the table — the small yes and the large yes — are the hardest to see while they are happening, because each of them is reasonable on its own. The test is simple: does the small one make the large one easier to say yes to?
examples: Here is the comparable, with its date and its scope.
That is the same fact in two frames; here is the total over three years.
A favour is not a gift. Here is the price of the order.
What you have already paid cannot be brought back by paying more.
sections.heading: Every technique and the honest version of the same request

The honest version of the same request

terms.example: The free trial was the foot in the door, and the yearly contract came next.
terms.gloss: A small, easy agreement that becomes the reason for a much larger one.

terms.example: The full package at 200,000 was the door in the face, and the single machine was the real order.
terms.gloss: A large request made first, so that the smaller request looks reasonable.

sections.body:
Six steps, in order. The first three are done before the meeting, on paper. The last three are done in the room, out loud. Each one is a sentence you can say without drama.

Steps one and two are your own numbers. The **best alternative to a negotiated agreement** — the BATNA — is the deal you will make if this deal does not happen: the other supplier, the other offer, the internal budget you would use instead, the date you would start again. Write it down before you go in. If it is not written down, it does not exist at the moment you need it, and that is exactly the moment the other side is pushing. The **walk-away price** is the number above which this deal is worse than your alternative, plus the cost of switching. Set it before, keep it to yourself, and do not move it in the conversation.

Step three is the frame. Ask what is being compared: the monthly cost, the total over three years, the cost per user, the cost per machine. Then ask where the deadline comes from — who sets the date, and what happens if the answer comes on Friday. Neither question accuses anybody, and both of them move the decision back to a place where it can be checked.

The last two steps are about time and about the record. Slow the decision down: *"I will answer in writing tomorrow"* is a normal sentence, and a decision that waits a day is a decision you made. And put the terms in writing: the price, the scope, the delivery, the date the terms change, the date the contract ends. The **sunk cost** is what you have already paid — the deposit, the setup, the months of testing. It is the most expensive trap in a renewal, because those months are gone whatever you decide now, and money that is already gone cannot be brought back by paying more.
examples: Before the meeting, I write down what I will do if this deal does not happen.
My walk-away price is set. I will not move it in the room.
Are we comparing the monthly cost or the total over three years?
I will answer in writing tomorrow morning.
sections.heading: How to negotiate without being moved
steps: Write down your alternative before the meeting: the best deal you will make if this deal does not happen, with the name of the other option and the date you would start.
Set your walk-away price from that alternative, add the cost of switching, and write the number down. Do not say it out loud, and do not change it in the room.
Name the frame out loud: "Are we comparing the monthly cost, the total over three years, or the cost per user?"
Ask where the deadline comes from: "Who sets the date, and what happens if the answer comes on Friday?"
Slow the decision down: "I will put that in writing and answer tomorrow morning."
Put the terms in writing: the price, the scope, the delivery, the date the terms change and the date the contract ends. Read them before you sign.

terms.example: Before the meeting he wrote down his BATNA: the other supplier, the price and the date.
terms.gloss: The best deal you can make if the deal in front of you does not happen.

terms.example: He set his walk-away price the week before, and he did not move it in the room.
terms.gloss: The price above which the deal is worse than your best alternative.

terms.example: The setup was paid, and the sunk cost was the argument to pay again.
terms.gloss: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, used as the reason to continue.

sections.body:
This article does not teach you to distrust every offer. A high price is not a trick. A real deadline is not a lie. A supplier who likes you is not manipulating you. Most of the people across the table are telling you the truth about most things, and most negotiations are ordinary work between two sides with real limits.

It does not make pressure illegitimate either. If the buyer has one week of budget left and you have one week of stock, the honest sentence — *"the price changes on Friday, here is the notice"* — is the right sentence to say, and the other side is allowed to act on it. The line drawn here is not between persuasion and honesty. It is between a request and a request with a hidden fact under it.

And it does not make you hard. Naming a technique is not an accusation, and none of the six steps asks you to walk away from good business. They ask you to know your own number before you are asked for it, so that the answer is yours.
examples: A real deadline is not a trick.
Both sides can be under pressure and still tell the truth.
Knowing your number before the meeting is preparation, not distrust.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
Use these at the moment you have to answer, not afterwards. The first four are for a buyer, the next three for a seller, the last three for a meeting room or an e-mail. No sentence here accuses the other side, and no sentence here gives up the decision.

The flatness is the point. A sentence that names a technique starts an argument about the technique, and you want the argument to be about the price, the terms and the date.
examples: What is the comparable for this, and what date does it come from?
How many are in stock, and when was that counted?
Is the Friday date a price change, or somebody's internal deadline?
We are the first company to buy this, so there is no customer of yours I can compare it with.
Here is the price list. The comparison you have is with a different scope, so let us compare the same scope.
The price changes on Friday; here is the notice, with its date and its reason.
The sample is free. The order is a separate decision, with its own terms.
Before we answer, can we agree what we are comparing?
Let me put that in writing and come back tomorrow morning.
Your alternative is a good one, and mine is this one. Let us compare the two.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
The pressure comes from the room the negotiation happens in. On a **sales floor** the price list is often not on the table, the seller has already answered the objection you were going to raise, and the machines on display are the easy ones. Nothing about that is dishonest. It is a prepared setting, and the person standing in it is often on a target.

In a **hiring room** the same structure appears: a salary band, a sign-on bonus with a date on it, a start date that is sooner than the notice period of the other job. An offer that expires is not a lie. It is still a decision, and a candidate who has another offer needs to know whether that date is a real one.

A **renewal call** is the same room with the history on your side of the table: the price change justified by a cost increase, the new plan that makes the old terms look generous, the two years of service used as the reason to sign for two more. And a **vendor's e-mail** carries the pressure without a voice in it: the discount that expires, the notice that arrives on Friday evening, the renewal that is cheaper only this week.

What changes when the person across the table is also under a target is the kind of answer they are able to give. A salesperson with a quarter to close, a manager with a vacancy to fill, a vendor with a cost increase to pass on: none of them is lying by nature, and all of them can change a number if they are given a reason better than the one they have. A person with a target can often be told yes more easily than a person with nothing to prove, and no more easily too. Knowing where the pressure comes from does not make it weaker. It tells you what to say: a reason, not a complaint.
examples: A deadline on a sales floor is a fact until somebody checks the date.
The offer that expires is still a decision, and I have to make it on the facts.
The two years of service are a reason to look at the renewal, not a reason to sign it.
sections.heading: Where the pressure comes from

item.summary: Persuasion is ordinary in a negotiation; the dark part is using it to hide the real price, the real stock or the real deadline. After reading this you can name nine techniques, say what the honest version of the same request is, and prepare the two things that protect you: your alternative and your walk-away price.
item.title: Dark Psychology in Business and Negotiation
